name: Beth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 27, and I lead electricians wiring and repairing homes and small businesses. I hold a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and the firm pays me above the usual rate. I live alone, have no children and keep ten months of expenses saved, separate from tools and holiday money. Every day I use approved AI to draft a handover from my notes, but the test sheet beside the screen is still my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful little tools can stay even if the big promises don't arrive. I use AI to turn my own rough job notes into a first draft every day, then check every line. I'd rather have a clean handover than win an argument about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable in that world. My pay is above the usual rate, I've got ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other electrical firms around here. I like my work, so I don't need a dramatic change to make my life feel successful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the installation and repair team. Starting now I'd carry on checking the AI-drafted handover against my test sheet before sending it to the office. During the first year I'd keep my present spending and work routine rather than buy equipment just because somebody calls it the next big thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little amused at how many arguments we'd have had for very little. I'd still enjoy trying a tool when I could see a use for it. My savings don't need a revolution to remain useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about leading the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching a younger electrician understand a fault rather than just copy my hands. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, but teaching makes me explain what I actually know. That's a good check on a person too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten months saved mean in your day-to-day life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can replace worn work boots without moving the rent money around. I live alone and don't have children, so my regular bills are fairly predictable. I keep the reserve separate from money for tools and holidays.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** even if the biggest AI promises came to little.
I'd value a checked **handover** more than winning an argument about the future.
think: My **higher pay** and ten months saved make my work and money feel comfortable.
Plenty of **nearby firms** give me options, though I like my current electrical work.
do: Keep leading **installations and repairs** through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI handovers** against my own test sheets before sending them.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity about useful tools and no need for dramatic change to feel secure.
S0.quote: I can replace worn work boots without moving the rent money around.
fieldNote: Her **financial calm** is supported by higher pay, ten months of expenses saved, predictable single-person bills and several nearby employers.
Her **daily AI use** stays tied to verified notes; she values understanding and teaching faults rather than credentials alone.

steps.text: Keep leading electrical jobs and checking daily AI handovers against test sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office stop copying the same details into three forms. I'd happily test a better way of preparing a repair visit, provided a person still checks the site information. More thinking work changing doesn't mean we stop caring what happens inside the customer's wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours and income would hold over the next few years. We have a full repair diary, and even fast planning doesn't pull old cable through a wall. Some office colleagues have more to worry about than I do; I can be honest about that without making myself their spokesperson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer the owner a six-week trial now, using the approved AI system to draft the next day's equipment lists from our checked job notes. I'd compare each draft with the actual visit and record anything missing before an order was made. During the first year I'd use the method only if that comparison showed fewer errors without cutting safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel positive about testing it, and secure in my own work. I'd be annoyed if a useful trial became an excuse to stop checking. Those are different feelings from fearing I can't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the trial saved no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner and drop it. I'm paid well enough not to need every experiment to prove I was clever. The point is a better repair visit, not keeping my favourite software busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to an office colleague who was worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what work was being changed and listen before offering an answer. I wouldn't promise that my busy repair diary meant their job was safe. If the firm offered teaching, I'd hope it happened in paid hours, but I can't promise the owner's decision.

say: I'd welcome less **duplicate paperwork** while keeping checks on site information.
I'd test tools against **real visits**, with attention to what happens inside the customer's wall.
think: I expect my **hours and income** to hold while the repair diary remains full.
I recognise **office colleagues** face more direct change without assuming my security proves theirs.
do: Offer a **six-week trial** now of AI equipment lists based on checked job notes.
Compare each **draft list** with real visits before ordering any equipment.
Continue the method during the **first year** only if errors fall and safety checks remain.
feel: **Calm** about her own livelihood, with interest in an experiment and concern for colleagues.
S1.quote: The point is a better repair visit, not keeping my favourite software busy.
fieldNote: She supports **earnings confidence** with a full physical repair diary while separating office exposure from work inside buildings.
Her **trial** has an evidence-based stop rule; neither enthusiasm nor her strong cushion requires the software to succeed.

steps.text: Trial AI equipment lists for six weeks and retain them only if checked errors fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 are two different stages of the same change. I'd tell the team to use the gap, not pretend physical work is protected forever. I'd also tell people to check an offer before handing in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own income could fall once firms start buying capable robots, even with a master electrician's licence. Ten months saved means I can take time over an offer, not that I can stop earning at 27. Plenty of nearby firms helps, though those firms could all be changing together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start adding 200 a month from my pay to the reserve now instead of booking an expensive holiday. I'd list actual advertised repair-team vacancies each month without leaving my present job. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply only for posts with stated pay and paid hours covering my bills, then compare written offers before deciding whether to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my future earnings, but not overwhelmed. I can afford to check a decision rather than make it on the pavement outside the yard. I'd rather use the reserve to buy thinking time than tell myself I can't be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by buying thinking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my hours fell, I could cover bills while checking other offers instead of taking the first wage somebody named. I wouldn't spend the reserve on a robot before I knew the price, maintenance costs and customer demand. Savings make a bad purchase possible too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still need your hands in the first year after 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running cables through occupied buildings, finding the fault and leaving everything tested. The planning could be done by a powerful system without the physical work vanishing that same day. I'd keep earning from that work while being honest about the robots coming later.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots following around 2031.
I'd urge the **team** to use the gap and compare offers rather than assume permanent physical protection.
think: My **income could fall** when firms buy capable robots, despite my licence and experience.
Ten months saved buys **decision time**, while nearby employers may all face the same changes.
do: Save another **200 monthly** now by postponing an expensive holiday.
Track actual **repair-team adverts** monthly while staying employed.
Apply after **2028** only for sufficient stated pay and paid hours, comparing written offers before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about future earnings, with resources to make considered decisions rather than rush.
S2.quote: Savings make a bad purchase possible too.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** changes the pace of decisions without making her immune to the physical robot phase or simultaneous employer changes.
The **vacancy plan** retains written pay and paid-hour conditions, while the first post-2028 year still includes physical electrical work.

steps.text: Save an extra 200 monthly instead of booking the expensive holiday
Apply after 2028 for posted repair-team roles with sufficient pay and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is useful time to turn experience into something another person can learn. I'd like apprentices to have good teaching before the thinking systems arrive in 2031. I'd still explain that robots around 2034 could change the hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own repair wages to remain secure over the next few years, so I can test another source of income without depending on it. Teaching apprentices interests me more than buying a machine I can't price properly. It wouldn't be immune to AI; I'd be testing whether people still pay for supervised practical help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my employer's permission and check the requirements for offering paid weekend practice sessions to apprentices. If allowed, I'd cap setup spending at 400 from spare earnings, leaving my emergency savings untouched, and advertise one supervised session a month on an isolated practice board with no live supply. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep my electrical job and continue sessions only if paid bookings covered their costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer future, but pleased to have room for a small test. I like the idea of a learner finally seeing why a fault happens. I'd judge the business by actual bookings, not by how much I enjoyed making the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the sessions attracted no paying learners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop after three sessions without enough paid bookings to cover costs. I'd still have my job and the emergency reserve, and the practice board could stay a teaching aid at home. I wouldn't spend more on apprentice teaching just to prove my first 400 was wise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach in person if thinking AI can explain anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly what I'd need to find out. Some learners may pay to have a person watch their hands and correct a mistake, but I don't know how many. Robots later could provide that help too, so I wouldn't call teaching a permanent shelter.

say: I'd use **five years** to turn practical experience into useful teaching for apprentices.
I'd explain that **robots around 2034** still change the hands-on side after thinking AI arrives.
think: I expect **near-term repair wages** to remain secure while I test a second income source.
I don't know whether learners will **pay** for practical teaching once powerful AI and later robots are available.
do: Check **employer permission** and requirements now before offering paid apprentice practice sessions.
Limit setup to **400** from spare earnings and advertise one monthly isolated-board session only if allowed.
Keep my **electrical job** after 2031 and continue sessions only when paid bookings cover costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, with enjoyment of a small teaching experiment she can afford to stop.
S3.quote: I wouldn't spend more on apprentice teaching just to prove my first 400 was wise.
fieldNote: Her **teaching sideline** is conditional on permission and requirements, with a fixed affordable cap and no live supply on the practice board.
Actual **paid bookings** decide continuation; she acknowledges AI and robots may compete with the proposed service rather than promising protected demand.

steps.text: Offer monthly apprentice practice only if permitted within a 400 spare-earnings setup cap
Keep the electrical job after 2031 while checking session costs against paid bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to train people properly and try tools without making every purchase a bet on survival. I'd still welcome competition that actually improves the work. I'd want apprentices told what is known and what is a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure about the next few years because my pay is good, my reserve is solid and there are plenty of local employers. I'd only be 37 in 2036 and around 40 when robots followed, so I can't talk as if retirement solves the endpoint. A secure present gives me time to try things, not a permanent exemption from change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and adding to my normal savings now. I'd test the same monthly practice session only with permission, the required checks and the 400 spare-earnings cap. In the first year after 2036 I'd review electrical wages and paid teaching bookings every quarter before putting further money into the sideline, keeping the emergency reserve separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own next few years. I can be interested in the future without having to put a brave face on the rent. I'd enjoy some of the time as well as prepare for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop treating the next few years as secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real fall in paid hours or the owner cancelling work for lack of customers. I'd change the plan then rather than quote today's full diary back at the bank. Confidence should have a reason you can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I still expect to earn, and I'm keeping cash rather than buying every machine somebody offers. My parents taught me that tools should earn their place. I'd apply the same rule to an AI subscription or a practice-board business.

say: I'd use the **decade** for proper teaching and practical experiments without treating every purchase as survival.
I'd tell **apprentices** clearly which claims are known and which are guesses.
think: Good **pay and reserves** make the next few years feel secure, with plenty of local employment options.
I'll still need earnings after **2036**, so present security isn't immunity from eventual automation.
do: Keep **working and saving** now without mixing the emergency reserve with sideline money.
Test **monthly teaching** only with permission, requirements checks and the 400 spare-earnings cap.
Review **wages and bookings** quarterly after 2036 before putting further money into teaching.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work and money, with room to enjoy life while preparing.
S4.quote: Confidence should have a reason you can check.
fieldNote: She anchors **calm** in pay, reserves and options, naming falling hours or cancelled work as evidence that would change her view.
The **common endpoint** remains explicit: she will not be retired at the AGI or robot dates, and teaching demand is never guaranteed.

steps.text: Keep electrical work and review actual wages quarterly after 2036
Continue ordinary saving while keeping the emergency reserve separate
Test permitted monthly apprentice sessions within the 400 spare-earnings setup cap

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because physical robots follow around 2031 before I've had long to test another income source. Honest paid-hour offers would help, along with time to try things while keeping my wages. I'd prefer useful work and good practical teaching to waiting for a promise that somebody else will pay my bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people would refuse to buy. A full savings account can make a foolish machine look affordable. I'd like us to compare real costs and actual customers before congratulating ourselves on being ready.

headlineQuote: A full savings account can make a foolish machine look affordable.
portrait: Beth is **27**, a highly skilled electrical team lead with a technical diploma and master's licence, higher pay and ten months saved.
She lives **alone**, has no children and uses checked AI handovers daily, with plenty of other local electrical firms available.
Her **short-timetable concern** centres on future earnings, while strong reserves allow written-offer comparisons without a rushed resignation.
Longer horizons permit **paid practical teaching** within spare earnings, with permission, cost limits and actual bookings required before continuation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to test another income source before capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid-hour offers** would help her judge employment options.
Time for **practical experiments** while maintaining wages would let her prepare without depending on untested income.
